open_questions: A single additional transit with precise duration and impact parameter would confirm whether higher-impact grazing EB model is preferred over flat-bottom planet; radial-velocity would rule out stellar companion.
dossier.public_summary: The 13.7-day 1.1% dip is grazing with a very poor density match and a 1960 ppm phase curve on a highly spotted M dwarf, plus a 25% odd-even difference without a planet-like secondary. No nearby star can produce the depth and the shape is better explained by a small grazing eclipsing binary on the target than by a 5 Earth-radius planet.

reasons.why: Flat-bottom sign is weak and grazing geometry explains it; high impact parameter grazing eclipse looks flat-bottomed with no odd/even or secondary difference, net favours stellar eclipse over planet.
Transit shape and duration_ratio=1.219 imply stellar density that is ~1.22x central; poor fit and density mismatch point to non-central stellar eclipse, not a planet.

Large odd/even depth difference (15.9 ccm and 26% difference) below 4-sigma formal threshold is consistent with noise but amplitude is substantial for a stable planet; combined with high b it supports binary viewed at twice period rather than planet.
Significant out-of-transit modulation at this period with amplitude ~18% of transit depth indicates spot/ellipsoidal binary variability, not expected for isolated planet.
Star is rapidly spotted variable; dip is not at a rotation multiple (signal_over_rotation=11.94) so no resonance argument remains, but variability explains phase-curve.
Independent scorer trained on confirmed planets rates this as very unlike planets (only ~6% of planets this low), consistent with multiple binary/grazing indicators.

No plausible neighbour within one TESS pixel that can cause 10790 ppm dip (0%-eclipse plausible), and inconclusive centroid does not prove off-target, so blend is ruled out and binary must be on target.
